terms.meaning: The idea that a market tends to behave a certain way at the same time each year, for example rising more often in April or falling more often in September.
terms.why: This whole study asks one question: are there calendar periods that reliably beat or lag the S&P 500's normal behavior?
terms.example: "Sell in May and go away" is a seasonality claim. It says May through October is usually weaker than the rest of the year.

terms.meaning: The data used to discover patterns. Here, that is the S&P 500 from January 2003 through December 2022.
terms.why: Patterns found in the same data used to search for them always look better than they really are. They must be checked on different data before you trust them.
terms.example: Finding that April rose in 16 of 20 years (2003–2022) is an in-sample result.

terms.meaning: Fresh data that played no part in discovering the patterns. Here, January 2023 through October 2, 2026.
terms.why: This is the honest test. If a pattern was real, it should keep showing up in data it has never seen.
terms.example: Checking whether April also beat a normal month in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 is an out-of-sample test.

terms.meaning: Add up the returns from every year and divide by the number of years.
terms.why: It shows the typical size of the move, but one huge year can drag it a long way.
terms.example: Returns of +2%, +3% and −1% average to +1.33%.

terms.meaning: The middle value after sorting the returns from lowest to highest.
terms.why: It isn't pulled around by one extreme year, so it shows what a 'normal' year looked like. When the median and average disagree a lot, a few unusual years are driving the average.
terms.example: For +2%, +3%, +1%, +2% and +15%, the average is +4.6% but the median is +2%. The +15% year is distorting the average.

terms.meaning: The share of years in which the period went the expected way: up for a bullish period, down for a bearish one.
terms.why: It is easy to understand but easy to over-read. The S&P 500 rises in most periods anyway, so a high win rate for a bullish window is less special than it sounds.
terms.example: Up in 16 of 20 years is an 80% win rate. But a random 10-day window in 2003–2022 was up about 62% of the time anyway.

terms.meaning: How much better or worse a period did than a normal or expected return over the same length of time.
terms.why: A market period that gained 2% may not be special if comparable periods normally gained 2.5%. Excess return separates a real calendar effect from the market's general upward drift.
terms.example: A return of +2% against a typical +1% is an excess return of +1 percentage point.

terms.meaning: The 'normal' return to compare against: the average return of every possible holding period of the same length in 2003–2022.
terms.why: It is the yardstick. A seasonal window only counts as special if it beats the baseline, not just zero.
terms.example: The 2003–2022 baseline for any 10-trading-day hold is +0.34%. A 10-day window averaging +1.42% beat it by +1.08 points.

terms.meaning: The market's general tendency to rise over time, regardless of the calendar.
terms.why: In a strong market almost every bullish window looks good. In 2023–2026 a random 20-day hold averaged +1.51%, against +0.69% in 2003–2022. That flatters every bullish rule tested in the newer period.
terms.example: If any 15-day period gained +1.1% on average in 2023–2026, a seasonal window gaining +1.5% beat the drift by only +0.4 points.

terms.meaning: The largest fall from a high point to a later low point within a period, even if the price recovered afterwards.
terms.why: It shows the pain you would have sat through. A month can end +2% yet have been down 6% along the way.
terms.example: Prices go 100 → 104 → 97 → 102. The maximum drawdown is (97 ÷ 104) − 1 = −6.7%, even though the period ended up +2%.

terms.meaning: A measure of how spread out the results are around their average.
terms.why: A large standard deviation means individual years vary a lot, so the average is less dependable.
terms.example: Monthly S&P returns in 2003–2022 had a standard deviation of about 4.3%. A typical month landed within roughly ±4.3% of the +0.7% average.

terms.meaning: A range of values that the true long-run average plausibly falls in, given the data. A 95% interval is built by a method that captures the true value 95% of the time.
terms.why: Small samples give wide ranges. If the range includes zero, the data can't rule out 'no real effect'.
terms.example: An average of +1.7% with a 95% interval of −0.5% to +3.8% still allows for no advantage at all.

terms.meaning: How surprising a result would be if there were no genuine seasonal advantage. A small p-value means the result would be unusual by luck alone.
terms.why: It helps judge whether a pattern could easily appear by chance. It is NOT the probability that the pattern is real, and it says nothing about how big or useful an effect is.
terms.example: A p-value of 0.36 means a result this good shows up about 36% of the time by luck. That is not strong evidence of a dependable seasonal advantage.

terms.meaning: A result is called 'significant' when its p-value falls below a threshold chosen in advance, commonly 0.05, after any needed correction for multiple tests.
terms.why: It is a filter against fooling yourself. 'Not significant' does not prove there is no effect; it means the data can't separate the effect from noise.
terms.example: Five of 120 windows had p < 0.05. That sounds good until you realise about 6 would be expected by chance.

terms.meaning: The expected share of 'discoveries' that are actually flukes. The Benjamini–Hochberg method adjusts p-values to keep that share below a chosen level.
terms.why: When you test 120 windows, some will look good by luck. FDR control keeps you from reporting a pile of flukes as findings.
terms.example: Controlling FDR at 10% means that, on average, at most 1 in 10 reported discoveries would be false.

terms.meaning: A p-value adjusted for false discovery rate. It is the smallest FDR level at which the result would count as a discovery.
terms.why: This study's rule was q ≤ 0.10 for 'Strong'. The best window had q = 0.64, so no window qualified.
terms.example: q = 0.64 means that calling this window a discovery would accept a false-discovery rate of about 64%.

terms.meaning: Shuffle the data in a way that destroys the pattern being tested, re-run the whole analysis thousands of times, and see how often the shuffled data does as well as the real data.
terms.why: It builds the 'luck' benchmark from the data itself and handles awkward situations, like overlapping windows, that standard formulas get wrong.
terms.example: Shifting each year's calendar by a random amount 2,000 times showed that the best of 120 random windows usually looks as good as the best real one.

terms.meaning: Compare a rule with fake 'rules' that use random dates instead of the real calendar dates, like a sugar pill in a drug trial.
terms.why: If randomly timed windows do just as well, the calendar timing added nothing.
terms.example: The bullish windows beat random windows in only about 64% of placebo draws (p = 0.36). That means random timing did about as well.

terms.meaning: Re-create many 'alternative histories' by drawing years at random, with replacement, from the real ones, then see how much the average moves around.
terms.why: It gives a confidence interval without assuming returns follow a neat bell curve.
terms.example: Resampling the 20 Aprils 10,000 times gives a range of plausible April averages.

terms.meaning: A measure from −1 to +1 of whether two rankings agree. +1 means identical order, 0 means no relationship, −1 means reversed.
terms.why: It tests whether rules that looked best in 2003–2022 also tended to do best in 2023–2026.
terms.example: A value of +0.15 means a faint tendency for historical winners to stay ahead, too weak to rely on.

terms.term: Rho (ρ), share of the historical edge
terms.meaning: The fraction of a rule's 2003–2022 advantage that reappeared in 2023–2026. It is calculated as the newer excess return divided by the historical excess return.
terms.why: It shows whether an effect persisted (ρ ≈ 1), weakened (between 0 and 1), vanished (≈ 0) or reversed (negative).
terms.example: A historical edge of +1.0 point and a newer edge of +0.5 points give ρ = 0.5: half the edge survived.

terms.meaning: How big a difference is, as opposed to whether it is statistically detectable. This study uses Cohen's d: the average excess return divided by its standard deviation.
terms.why: A tiny effect can be 'significant' with enough data, and a large one can be 'not significant' with too little. Size tells you whether it would matter in practice.
terms.example: An average excess of +1% with a standard deviation of 2% gives d = 0.5, a moderate effect.

terms.meaning: Accidentally using information that would not have been known at the time, such as tomorrow's price, when simulating a past decision.
terms.why: It makes backtests look far better than real trading could ever be. This project blocks it in code: the data handler refuses any request for a future price.
terms.example: Deciding on Monday to buy because you 'know' Friday's close is higher is look-ahead bias.

terms.meaning: Tuning a rule so closely to past data that it captures random noise instead of a real pattern.
terms.why: Overfit rules look excellent historically and then fail on new data. That is why this study froze its rules before testing them on 2023–2026.
terms.example: Moving a window's start from Apr 16 to Apr 13 because that worked better in the past would be overfitting.

terms.meaning: Drawing conclusions only from things that survived, and ignoring those that dropped out.
terms.why: It matters less here, because this study looks at the S&P 500 index as published. It matters a lot when people study only today's companies, or only the strategies they still remember.
terms.example: Judging fund managers using only funds still open today ignores the ones that closed after doing badly.

terms.meaning: Adjusting the evidence bar when many things are tested at once, because some will look good by chance.
terms.why: Testing 120 windows at the 5% level would produce about 6 flukes even if no seasonality exists. Corrections such as FDR and family-wise permutation tests account for this.
terms.example: Flip 120 coins and a few will land heads 5 times in a row. That doesn't make them special coins.

terms.meaning: A fixed holding period defined by a calendar start date and a number of trading days, for example 'start Apr 16, hold 10 trading days'.
terms.why: Each window is a rule tested the same way every year. Because it counts trading days, the exact end date shifts by a day or two between years.
terms.example: Apr 16 + 10 trading days: buy at the close before Apr 16 and sell at the close about two weeks later, usually around Apr 29.

terms.meaning: Evaluating each simulated decision using only data that existed on that date.
terms.why: It is the guard against look-ahead bias. Every trade in this study was calculated from a data view that physically contained no later prices.
terms.example: To judge a trade that exits on Jul 22, 2024, the program can see prices up to Jul 22, 2024 and nothing after.

terms.meaning: A day the stock market is open. There are about 21 in a month and 252 in a year.
terms.why: Windows are measured in trading days so every year holds the same number of market sessions.
terms.example: "15 td" is about three calendar weeks.

terms.meaning: The simple difference between two percentages.
terms.why: It avoids confusion. Going from 2% to 3% is +1 percentage point, but a 50% relative increase.
terms.example: An average of +2.25% falling to +1.48% is a drop of 0.77 pp.

terms.meaning: The chance that at least one of all the windows tested would look this good by luck alone.
terms.why: It is the strictest multiple-testing check. The best window's FWER p-value was 0.40: a fluke this good happens 40% of the time.
terms.example: If 120 random windows usually include one with a t-statistic around 3, a real window scoring 3.15 is not remarkable.

terms.meaning: How many 'standard errors' an average sits away from zero. A larger value means stronger evidence that the average is not zero.
terms.why: It is the basis of the t-test p-value. With 20 years of data, a t of about 2.1 corresponds to p ≈ 0.05 before any multiple-testing correction.
terms.example: An average excess of +1.7% with a standard error of 0.55% gives t ≈ 3.1.

formulas.name: Period return
symbols: closing price on the last trading day before the period starts
closing price on the last day of the period
formulas.reading: Positive means the index rose over the period.
formulas.limits: These are price returns. They ignore dividends (about 1.5–2% a year), trading costs, slippage and taxes.

formulas.name: Monthly return (heat-map cells)
formulas.formula: r_month = Close(last trading day of month) ÷ Close(last trading day of previous month) − 1
formulas.reading: Teal cells are gains and red cells are losses; the darker the cell, the bigger the move.
formulas.limits: The first month of each data file (Jan 2003, Jan 2023) starts from that day's open because the file has no earlier close, as the frozen study did. October 2026 is incomplete and is never given a monthly return.

formulas.name: Excess return
symbols: the rule's average return across years
the average return of ALL holding periods of the same length in 2003–2022
formulas.worked: Apr 16 + 10 td averaged +1.42% (2003–2022). The 10-day baseline was +0.34%, so excess = +1.08 pp.
formulas.reading: Above 0 means better than an ordinary period of the same length; below 0 means worse.
formulas.limits: The baseline depends on the market environment. 2023–2026 rose faster than 2003–2022, so excess measured against the old baseline flatters bullish rules in the newer period.

formulas.name: Win rate
formulas.formula: win rate = number of years in the expected direction ÷ number of years
formulas.reading: Higher is better, but compare it with the base rate. Random windows of the same length were up 58–66% of the time.
formulas.limits: With 3–4 years, one year moves the win rate by 25–33 points. A perfect 4-of-4 is consistent with a true rate anywhere from about 40% to 100%.

formulas.name: Maximum drawdown
formulas.formula: MDD = min over the period of ( Price ÷ highest price so far − 1 )
symbols: the running peak, including the entry price
formulas.reading: Closer to 0 is calmer. A large negative number means a painful dip along the way.
formulas.limits: This study uses daily closes, so falls that happen within a single day are not counted.

formulas.name: t-statistic and p-value
formulas.reading: A bigger |t| gives a smaller p, which means the result would be more surprising by luck alone.
formulas.limits: This assumes years are independent and roughly bell-shaped. It does not correct for testing 120 windows; that is what the q-value and permutation tests do.

formulas.name: Benjamini–Hochberg q-value
formulas.formula: q(k) = min over j ≥ k of ( p(j) × m ÷ j ), with p-values sorted from smallest p(1) to largest p(m)
formulas.worked: Best p = 0.0053, m = 120, rank 1 → 0.0053 × 120 ÷ 1 = 0.64 (after taking the running minimum).
formulas.reading: q ≤ 0.10 was the bar for 'Strong'. Lower is better.
formulas.limits: It assumes tests are independent or positively related. Overlapping windows are positively related, which this method tolerates.

formulas.name: Rho (share of the historical edge)
formulas.worked: Jul 1 + 15 td: newer excess +0.97 pp ÷ historical excess +1.74 pp = 0.56.
formulas.limits: When the historical edge is tiny (for example December, +0.20 pp), ρ swings wildly and means little.

formulas.name: Placebo percentile
formulas.formula: percentile = share of 10,000 random-date windows that the real rule beat in its expected direction
formulas.worked: Apr 16 + 10 td beat 76% of random windows of the same length in 2023–2026.
formulas.reading: 50% means the calendar added nothing. 95% or more would be notable.
formulas.limits: With 3–4 years, percentiles bounce around a lot from one year's result.
